module_title: Reproduction and Breeding in Dairy Cattle

lessons.title: Anatomy and physiology of the reproductive system
lessons.body:
The cow's reproductive system has four main parts: ovaries, oviducts, uterus, and vagina. The ovaries are two almond-sized organs that produce eggs (ova) and hormones like estrogen and progesterone. Each month, a follicle on an ovary matures and releases an egg during ovulation. The oviduct is a tube that catches the egg and is where fertilization happens if sperm are present. The uterus is a muscular organ with two horns where the fetus grows. The cervix is a tight valve that seals the uterus during pregnancy and opens during heat and calving. The vagina is the birth canal and where the bull deposits semen.

In a healthy cow, the estrous cycle repeats every 18 to 24 days (average 21 days). The cycle has four stages: proestrus (follicle grows), estrus (heat, standing to be mounted), metestrus (ovulation occurs 12-16 hours after heat ends), and diestrus (corpus luteum forms and produces progesterone to maintain pregnancy if fertilized). If not pregnant, the corpus luteum breaks down after about 17 days, and the cycle restarts.

Practical signs of heat include standing still when other cows mount her, clear mucus from the vulva, restlessness, and bellowing. In Africa, heat detection is often poor because cows are not observed closely. Train workers to watch for heat twice daily for 20 minutes, especially early morning and evening. Use tail chalk or heat detector patches. A cow not showing heat for over 60 days after calving may have a problem; consult a vet.

Nutrition affects reproduction. Cows need adequate energy, protein, minerals (especially phosphorus and selenium), and vitamins (A, D, E). Underfeeding delays puberty and prolongs the time to first heat after calving. In many African smallholder farms, supplementing with dairy meal and mineral blocks improves heat expression and conception rates. Keep records of calving dates and heat dates to track cycle regularity. A simple calendar or notebook works. Healthy reproduction means a calf per cow per year, which is the goal for profitable dairy farming.

lessons.title: Estrus detection and synchronization protocols
lessons.body:
Detecting heat (estrus) accurately is critical for timely insemination. A cow's heat lasts 12 to 18 hours, and ovulation occurs 12 to 16 hours after heat ends. The best time to inseminate is 12 hours after heat is first seen (the AM/PM rule: if seen in morning, inseminate in evening; if seen in evening, inseminate next morning). Miss it, and you wait another 21 days. In Africa, where labor is limited, use simple tools: apply tail chalk daily and check for rubbing off; use heat detector patches (e.g., Kamar) that change color when mounted. Observe cows for 20 minutes twice daily, ideally at dawn and dusk when mounting activity peaks.

Synchronization protocols allow you to control when cows come into heat, so you can inseminate many cows on the same day. A common protocol is Ovsynch: inject GnRH on day 0, prostaglandin on day 7, GnRH on day 9, and inseminate 16-20 hours after the second GnRH (day 10). This works even if the cow is not showing heat. Another protocol uses a progesterone-releasing device (e.g., CIDR) inserted for 7 days, with prostaglandin given at removal. These protocols require veterinary supervision and may cost $10-20 per cow for hormones. They are best for farms with many cows and limited labor for heat detection.

For smallholder farms, simpler methods include using a bull with a chin-ball marker or vasectomized bull to detect heat. Keep a record of all heats and inseminations. If a cow returns to heat 18-24 days after insemination, she likely did not conceive. Synchronization can help group calvings, making calf management and feeding easier. However, ensure cows are cycling and in good body condition (score 2.5-3.5 on a 5-point scale) before starting any protocol. Poor nutrition will reduce success. Always consult an experienced AI technician or vet before using hormones.

lessons.title: Artificial insemination techniques
lessons.body:
Artificial insemination (AI) is the manual placement of semen into a cow's reproductive tract. It allows use of genetically superior bulls without keeping a bull on the farm, reducing disease risk and inbreeding. To do AI, you need: a liquid nitrogen tank to store semen at -196Â°C, an AI gun, thawing equipment (thermos with warm water at 35-37Â°C), plastic sheaths, gloves, and a breeding crate or head gate. Semen straws are thawed for 30-40 seconds in warm water, then loaded into the AI gun. The technician inserts a gloved hand into the rectum to guide the cervix, then passes the AI gun through the cervix and deposits semen into the uterus. The whole process takes 3-5 minutes per cow.

Proper timing is key: inseminate 12 hours after heat is first observed. If using synchronization, follow the protocol exactly. Handle semen carefully: never expose to sunlight, keep thawing water clean, and use straws immediately after thawing. Poor handling kills sperm. In Africa, many AI technicians are trained by government or private organizations. Costs range from $5 to $20 per insemination, plus semen cost. Success rate (conception) is typically 40-60% in well-managed herds, but can be lower if heat detection is poor or nutrition is inadequate.

For smallholders, AI can be done by a trained technician who visits the farm. Alternatively, learn to do it yourself through a short course. Always check the semen straw for the bull's ID and breed. After insemination, record the date, bull name, and technician. Watch for return to heat 18-24 days later. If she returns, repeat. If not, she may be pregnant. AI has revolutionized dairy breeding in Africa, allowing farmers to access top genetics from Europe, USA, and local breeds adapted to heat and disease. Use AI combined with good record-keeping for best results.

lessons.title: Pregnancy diagnosis and management
lessons.body:
After insemination, you need to know if the cow is pregnant. Early diagnosis saves money and time. Methods include: (1) Non-return to heat: if a cow does not show heat 21 days after breeding, she may be pregnant. But this is only 50-60% accurate. (2) Rectal palpation: a veterinarian or trained technician feels the uterus through the rectum. This can be done from 35-45 days after breeding. They feel for a fluid-filled uterus, a placentome (button-like structure), or a slipping membrane. (3) Ultrasound: from 28 days, a vet can see the embryo and heartbeat. This is more accurate but requires equipment. (4) Blood or milk tests: measure pregnancy-associated glycoproteins (PAGs) from 28 days. These tests are available in some African labs and cost $5-10 per sample. (5) Palpation of the middle uterine artery: a faint pulse (fremitus) can be felt from 4-5 months.

Once pregnancy is confirmed, manage the cow carefully. Provide a balanced diet: increase energy and protein in the last 2 months (steaming up) to support calf growth and prepare for lactation. Avoid stressing the cow: no rough handling, no long treks. Keep her away from bulls to prevent injury. Vaccinate against diseases like brucellosis and leptospirosis, which cause abortion. Deworm regularly. Monitor body condition: aim for score 3.0-3.5 at calving. If she is too thin, she may have a weak calf and low milk yield.

Pregnancy lasts about 280 days (9 months and 1 week). Keep a calendar: mark breeding date, expected calving date, and dry-off date (60 days before calving). Dry off the cow by stopping milking abruptly or gradually. Check for mastitis before dry-off. In the last month, watch for signs of calving: enlarged udder, relaxed pelvic ligaments, and mucus discharge. Have a calving kit ready: clean towels, iodine, gloves, and a rope. If the cow goes past 285 days without calving, consult a vet. Good pregnancy management ensures a healthy calf and a productive next lactation.

lessons.title: Genetic selection and breeding goals
lessons.body:
Genetic selection means choosing which cows and bulls to breed to improve the next generation. In dairy, the main goals are: high milk yield, good milk quality (butterfat and protein), disease resistance, heat tolerance, and good fertility. In Africa, where heat and diseases are major challenges, select for cows that can produce well under local conditions. Crossbreeds (e.g., Holstein-Friesian x Zebu) often perform better than pure exotic breeds because they combine high yield with hardiness. Local breeds like Boran, Sahiwal, and Ankole have good heat tolerance and tick resistance.

To select a bull for AI, look at his proof: milk yield of daughters, fertility, and calving ease. In Africa, use semen from bulls evaluated in similar environments. Many AI companies provide catalogs with bull rankings. For cows, keep records of milk yield per lactation, calving interval, and health. Cull cows that repeatedly fail to conceive, have chronic mastitis, or produce very little milk. Replace them with heifers from your best cows. Selection is slow: it takes generations to see major changes. But even small improvements compound.

Breeding goals should match your market. If you sell to a milk processor, they may pay based on fat and protein content. If you sell fresh milk locally, volume matters. Write down your goals: e.g., "Increase average milk yield from 8 to 12 liters per day in 5 years." Then choose bulls whose daughters produce more milk. Avoid inbreeding: never mate a bull to his own daughters. Keep a herd register with each animal's ID, sire, dam, and performance. In community breeding programs, farmers can share a superior bull or pool funds for AI. This is common in Kenya, Ethiopia, and Tanzania. Remember: genetics is only 30% of success; 70% is management (feeding, health, housing). Without good management, even the best genetics will fail.

lessons.title: Calving management and assistance
lessons.body:
Calving is the most critical time for the cow and calf. Most cows calve without help, but you should be prepared. Signs of imminent calving: udder fills with milk 1-2 days before, pelvic ligaments relax (tail head looks sunken), vulva swells, and the cow becomes restless, separating from the herd. Move her to a clean, dry calving pen with fresh bedding. Provide water and hay. Check her every 2 hours. Normal calving has three stages: (1) dilation of the cervix (2-6 hours), (2) expulsion of the calf (30 minutes to 2 hours), and (3) passing of the placenta (2-12 hours).

Assist only if needed. If the cow strains for over 2 hours without progress, or if you see the water bag but no calf after 1 hour, check the position. Wash your hands and the cow's vulva with soap and water. Wear clean gloves. Feel for the calf's head and front legs. Normally, two front hooves and the head come first (like a diver). If the calf is backwards (tail first) or legs back, you may need to correct it. Use gentle traction with ropes on the legs, pulling when the cow strains. Never pull hard or twist. If you cannot correct it, call a vet immediately. After the calf is born, clear its nose and mouth of mucus. If not breathing, rub its chest and tickle its nose with a straw. Dip the navel in iodine (7%) to prevent infection.

Let the cow lick the calf; this stimulates circulation and bonding. Ensure the calf suckles colostrum within 2 hours. Colostrum is rich in antibodies; without it, the calf will likely die. If the cow won't let it suckle, milk her and feed the calf with a clean bottle or esophageal tube. Give 2-4 liters in the first 6 hours. Watch for retained placenta: if not passed within 12 hours, consult a vet. After calving, provide the cow with warm water, hay, and a laxative feed (e.g., bran mash). Monitor for milk fever (staggering, cold ears) and treat with calcium. Keep records: calving date, calf sex, and any difficulties. Good calving management saves calves and keeps cows productive.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Dairy Reproduction & Breeding in African Herds

This practical reference is written for the commercial dairy operator, farm manager, and extension officer working in African production systems â from zero-grazing units in Kenya's Kiambu County to pasture-based herds in Zimbabwe's Mashonaland and mixed crop-livestock farms in Ethiopia's highlands. The goal is simple: turn reproductive biology into money. Every empty day beyond 85â90 days post-calving costs you feed, labour, and lost milk. Every failed insemination costs semen, technician fees, and another 21 days of waiting. This module gives you the numbers, the protocols, and the checkpoints to tighten your herd's reproductive performance.

1. Anatomy & Physiology â What You Must Know to Act

The cow's reproductive tract is a sequence of organs that each impose a timing constraint on your management. The ovaries produce the ova and the hormones (oestrogen, progesterone) that drive the cycle. The oviduct is where fertilisation occurs. The uterus (with its two horns) is where the embryo implants and the calf develops. The cervix is the muscular gate the insemination catheter must pass through. The vagina and vulva are the entry point and the visible indicator of oestrus.

The oestrous cycle averages 21 days (range 18â24). Oestrus â standing heat â lasts 8â18 hours in well-fed temperate breeds but is often shorter and less obvious in heat-stressed or underfed African herds. Ovulation occurs 10â14 hours after the end of standing oestrus. This is why the AM/PM rule matters: a cow seen in standing heat in the morning should be inseminated that afternoon; one seen in the afternoon should be inseminated the next morning. Sperm must be in the oviduct before ovulation, and frozen-thawed sperm needs 6â12 hours to capacitate. Timing is not optional.

Post-calving, the uterus needs 30â40 days to involute. The first ovulation typically occurs 15â30 days after calving, but the first heat is often silent. This is the "phantom heat" trap. A cow that calves and shows no heat by 60 days is a financial alarm, not a cow to "wait and see."

2. Estrus Detection & Synchronisation â The Economics

In African smallholder and medium-scale dairy systems, poor oestrus detection is the single largest cause of extended calving intervals. Studies across East Africa consistently report detection rates below 50% on many farms. The cost is stark: at 21 days per missed cycle, a cow missed twice adds 42 days open â roughly 300â400 litres of milk lost at 8â10 litres/day, plus extra feed and AI costs.

Practical detection tools that work in African conditions:

  • Tail paint or chalk: cheap, effective, and works with grazing herds. Re-apply every 2â3 days.
  • Heat mount detectors (Kamar): useful but require daily observation and clean application.
  • Visual observation: 20â30 minutes, 3â4 times daily, ideally early morning and late evening when heat behaviour peaks.
  • Bull teaser with chin-ball harness: the gold standard where a vasectomised or penile-deviated bull is available.

Synchronisation protocols allow you to schedule AI, reduce detection labour, and batch calvings â a major business advantage for labour planning and milk supply contracts. The two most practical protocols for African dairy herds are the Ovsynch and the Prostaglandin (PGF2Î±) single-injection protocol for cycling cows.

Table 1. Common oestrus synchronisation protocols for dairy cattle in African conditions
Protocol Day schedule Best for Approx. cost/cow (USD) Conception rate (typical)
PGF2Î± single injection Inject on Day 0; observe heat 48â72 h; AI at 72â80 h Cycling cows with a palpable corpus luteum 3â6 45â55%
Ovsynch (GnRHâPGFâGnRH) GnRH d0; PGF d7; GnRH d9; timed AI 16â20 h later Anoestrous or hard-to-detect cows; fixed-time AI 12â20 35â45%
Double PGF2Î± (11-day interval) PGF d0; PGF d11; AI at observed heat or 72â80 h Herds with poor heat detection 6â12 50â60%
CIDR / PRID + PGF Insert d0; PGF at removal d7; AI 48â56 h Anoestrous cows; high-value animals 15â25 45â55%

Sources: Adapted from FAO Artificial Insemination in Cattle (2011); ILRI Reproductive Performance of Dairy Cattle in East Africa technical briefs; and field data from Kenyan and Ethiopian dairy cooperatives. Costs are indicative and vary by country and supplier.

3. Artificial Insemination â Technique That Protects Your Investment

AI is the most powerful genetic tool available to the African dairy farmer â but only if the technique is right. A straw of sexed or conventional semen costs USD 5â40 depending on breed and source. Wasted doses destroy profitability.

Thawing: 35â37Â°C water bath for 30â45 seconds. Never thaw in your pocket, never use a thermos with warm water that cools, never re-freeze. Thaw one straw at a time. Use within 10â15 minutes.

Handling: Keep the AI gun warm (use a glove or insulated sleeve). Wipe the vulva clean. Insert the gun at a 30â45Â° angle to clear the pelvic rim, then level off and advance through the cervix using gentle rotation. Deposit in the body of the uterus. Do not force. If the cervix cannot be passed, stop â forcing causes trauma and infection.

Timing: AM/PM rule. Inseminate 12â18 hours after the onset of standing heat. If using timed AI, follow the protocol exactly.

Table 2. Key reproductive performance benchmarks for African dairy herds
Parameter Target Action threshold Business impact if missed
Calving interval 365â400 days >420 days Lost lactation days; reduced lifetime yield
Days open 85â110 days >120 days Extra feed, AI, and labour costs
First-service conception rate >50% <40% More straws, more technician visits
Services per conception 1.5â2.0 >2.5 Direct cost per pregnancy rises sharply
Heat detection rate >70% <50% Silent heats; missed cycles; extended intervals
Age at first calving 24â28 months >30 months Delayed income; higher rearing cost per litre
Calf mortality to weaning <5% >10% Lost replacement stock; genetic loss

Sources: ILRI Dairy Cattle Breeding and Reproductive Performance (2019); Kenya Dairy Board extension guidelines; FAO Guidelines for Dairy Cattle Breeding (2010). Thresholds are indicative for tropical and sub-tropical African conditions.

4. Pregnancy Diagnosis & Management

Pregnancy diagnosis (PD) is a cash-flow tool. Every day a non-pregnant cow stays unidentified is a day of lost income. Options in African settings:

  • Rectal palpation: reliable from 35â45 days post-AI. Requires a trained technician or vet. Low cost, high skill requirement.
  • Ultrasound: reliable from 28â30 days. Higher equipment cost but faster and more accurate; increasingly available in peri-urban African dairies.
  • Milk progesterone tests: useful for herd-level screening; not a substitute for individual PD.
  • Chemical tests (e.g., PAG-based): blood or milk tests from 28â30 days; good for remote farms.

Once confirmed pregnant, the cow enters a management phase that protects the pregnancy: maintain body condition score (BCS) 3.0â3.5, avoid heat stress, control parasites, and ensure adequate minerals (especially selenium, copper, and iodine). Re-check at 90â120 days to catch late embryonic loss. Dry off 60 days before calving and manage the transition period carefully â this is where most metabolic and reproductive problems begin.

5. Genetic Selection & Breeding Goals â Business First

In Africa, the best breed is the one that fits your system, not the one that wins a show. A Holstein that produces 30 litres on a European diet may produce 12 litres and struggle to conceive on a smallholder ration. Selection goals should be driven by your market:

  • Liquid milk market (peri-urban): prioritise milk yield, udder conformation, and mastitis resistance.
  • Cheese/butter market: prioritise fat and protein percentage.
  • Heat-stressed lowland systems: prioritise heat tolerance, tick resistance, and fertility (crossbreeds with Boran, Sahiwal, or Friesian-Sahiwal crosses).
  • Feed-limited systems: prioritise feed efficiency and moderate frame size.

Use AI sires with proven proofs â Interbull, national evaluations, or regional bull proofs from Kenya's KAGRC, Ethiopia's EIAR, or South Africa's SA Stud Book. Record every insemination, every calving, and every lactation. Without records, genetic selection is guesswork. With records, it is a business decision.

6. Calving Management & Assistance

Most calvings need no help. Intervene only when the cow has been in active labour for more than 2 hours without progress, or when the presentation is abnormal. Clean hands, clean equipment, and gentle traction in line with the cow's contractions. Never pull with a tractor or vehicle. After calving, check the placenta (should pass within 12 hours), monitor for metritis, and ensure the calf receives colostrum within the first 2 hours â 10% of body weight.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Zoonoses & Drug Residues

Brucellosis, leptospirosis, and Q-fever are occupational risks for anyone handling reproductive tracts, placentas, or aborted fetuses. Always wear disposable gloves and arm-length sleeves during AI, PD, and calving assistance. Wash hands and arms thoroughly with soap and disinfectant after every procedure. Never consume unpasteurised milk from a herd with a history of abortion. Dispose of placentas and aborted material by deep burial or incineration â never feed to dogs or leave accessible to other animals. Observe milk and meat withdrawal periods for all hormones, antibiotics, and prostaglandins used in synchronisation protocols. Failure to do so can lead to drug residues in milk, rejected deliveries, and loss of market access.

7. Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Observe heat 3â4 times daily for 20â30 minutes, especially early morning and late evening.
  2. Apply tail paint or chalk every 2â3 days on all cows eligible for breeding.
  3. Follow the AM/PM rule: inseminate 12â18 hours after onset of standing heat.
  4. Thaw semen correctly: 35â37Â°C for 30â45 seconds; use within 15 minutes.
  5. Record every AI, heat, and calving â no record, no genetic progress.
  6. Pregnancy-check all bred cows by 35â60 days; re-check at 90â120 days.
  7. Target days open <110 and calving interval <400 days; act on any cow exceeding 120 days open.
  8. Wear gloves and disinfect during all reproductive procedures; observe drug withdrawal periods.

8. Further Reading

  • FAO â Artificial Insemination in Cattle (free training manual)
  • ILRI â Dairy Cattle Breeding and Reproductive Performance in East Africa
  • Kenya Animal Genetic Resources Centre (KAGRC) â semen and breeding services
  • Dairy Africa â practical extension resources for African dairy farmers
  • WOAH (OIE) â animal health and zoonoses guidelines

Bottom line: Reproduction is the engine of dairy profitability. A cow that does not conceive does not pay. Fix heat detection first, tighten AI technique second, and let records drive your genetic decisions. In African conditions, the farms that win are not the ones with the fanciest breeds â they are the ones with the tightest reproductive management.

quiz.q: What is the average length of the estrous cycle in a cow?
quiz.explanation: The estrous cycle in cattle averages 21 days, ranging from 18 to 24 days.

quiz.q: Which hormone is responsible for maintaining pregnancy?
quiz.explanation: Progesterone from the corpus luteum maintains the uterine lining for pregnancy.

quiz.q: What is the best time to inseminate a cow after observing heat?
quiz.explanation: The AM/PM rule recommends insemination 12 hours after heat is first seen for optimal conception.

quiz.q: Which of these is a primary sign of estrus in cattle?
quiz.explanation: Standing still when mounted by other cows is the most reliable sign of heat.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a synchronization protocol?
options: A) To make cows produce more milk
B) To control when cows come into heat
D) To increase calf birth weight
quiz.explanation: Synchronization allows groups of cows to be inseminated at a predetermined time.

quiz.q: In the Ovsynch protocol, when is prostaglandin given?
quiz.explanation: In Ovsynch, prostaglandin is injected on day 7 to regress the corpus luteum.

quiz.q: What temperature should water be for thawing semen straws?
quiz.explanation: Semen straws are thawed in water at 35-37Â°C for 30-40 seconds to maintain sperm viability.

quiz.q: How long should a semen straw be thawed?
quiz.explanation: Thawing for 30-40 seconds in warm water ensures proper temperature without damaging sperm.

quiz.q: Where is semen deposited during artificial insemination?
quiz.explanation: Semen is deposited into the uterus through the cervix for fertilization to occur.

quiz.q: What is the typical conception rate for AI in well-managed herds?
quiz.explanation: Conception rates with AI usually range from 40% to 60% in good management conditions.

quiz.q: Which method can diagnose pregnancy as early as 28 days?
quiz.explanation: Ultrasound and blood tests for pregnancy-associated glycoproteins (PAGs) can detect pregnancy from about 28 days.

quiz.q: What is the average gestation length in dairy cattle?
quiz.explanation: The average gestation period for cows is about 280 days (9 months and 1 week).

quiz.q: When should a cow be dried off before calving?
quiz.explanation: Dry off the cow 60 days (2 months) before expected calving to allow udder rest and regeneration.

quiz.q: Which mineral is important for reproduction and is often deficient in African soils?
quiz.explanation: Phosphorus deficiency is common in many African soils and can impair fertility.

quiz.q: What is the recommended body condition score for a cow at calving?
quiz.explanation: A body condition score of 2.5-3.5 on a 5-point scale is ideal for calving and lactation.

quiz.q: Which breed is known for heat tolerance and tick resistance in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Sahiwal is a Zebu breed adapted to tropical conditions with good heat and tick resistance.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of genetic selection in dairy?
quiz.explanation: Genetic selection aims to improve multiple traits including yield, health, and fertility.

quiz.q: Why is inbreeding avoided in dairy cattle breeding?
options: B) It causes genetic defects and reduces fertility
quiz.explanation: Inbreeding leads to reduced genetic diversity, increased genetic defects, and lower fertility.

quiz.q: What percentage of success in dairy farming is attributed to genetics?
quiz.explanation: Genetics contributes about 30% to success, while management (feeding, health, housing) is 70%.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of imminent calving?
quiz.explanation: Relaxed pelvic ligaments and reduced appetite are common signs that calving is near.

quiz.q: How long should you wait before assisting a cow that is straining during calving?
quiz.explanation: If a cow strains for over 2 hours without progress, assistance may be needed.

quiz.q: What is the normal presentation of a calf during birth?
options: A) Head first, front legs forward
quiz.explanation: The normal birth position is head first with both front legs extended forward.

quiz.q: Why is colostrum important for the newborn calf?
quiz.explanation: Colostrum provides energy, antibodies, and growth factors essential for the calf's health.

quiz.q: Within how many hours should a calf receive colostrum?
quiz.explanation: Calves should receive colostrum within the first 6 hours of life for maximum antibody absorption.

quiz.q: What should you dip the newborn calf's navel in?
quiz.explanation: Dipping the navel in 7% iodine prevents infection.

quiz.q: What is a common metabolic disorder after calving?
quiz.explanation: Milk fever (hypocalcemia) is a common post-calving disorder caused by low blood calcium.

quiz.q: Which record is important for tracking reproduction?
quiz.explanation: Keeping records of calving, heat, and insemination dates helps manage reproduction effectively.

quiz.q: What is the recommended observation time for heat detection?
quiz.explanation: Observing cows for 20 minutes twice daily, especially at dawn and dusk, improves heat detection.

quiz.q: Which tool can help detect heat in cows?
quiz.explanation: Tail chalk and heat detector patches are practical tools for identifying mounted cows.

quiz.q: What is the goal of a breeding program in dairy?
options: A) One calf per cow per year
B) Two calves per cow per year
C) One calf every two years
quiz.explanation: The target is one calf per cow per year to maintain productivity and profitability.
